blocks.content: In the earlier Classes topic, you built a Car blueprint. But a blueprint alone never drove anywhere, printed anything, or ran out of fuel. The moment you write "new Car(...)", something real appears in memory: an object.

This topic is entirely about that "real thing": how many of them you can create from one class, how to tell two objects apart even when their data looks identical, and what actually happens in memory when you copy a reference instead of creating a fresh object.
1. Introduction & Why It Matters
An object is a concrete, in-memory instance created from a class. If a class is the blueprint, an object is one specific thing built from it, occupying real memory, with its own current field values.

A class only describes a shape. Without objects, you would have no way to represent "this specific car parked outside" separately from "that specific car in the garage", every car would collapse into one shared description with no independent state. Objects solve this by giving each instance its own private slice of memory: two Car objects built from the same class can have completely different fuel levels, brands, and identities, and changing one never touches the other.
2. Real-Life Analogy
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1784847662914-12663535.png
blocks.alt: Alice, Bob and Carol as three distinct Human objects sharing one Human class

blocks.content: Picture three people in a room: Alice, Bob, and Carol. All three are humans, built from the same general "Human" template, two arms, one heartbeat, the ability to speak. But each one is undeniably a separate, distinct individual. That is precisely what "object" means in code: the class Human describes what every human has in common, while Alice, Bob, and Carol are three separate objects, each with their own name, age, and mood at any given moment.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1784847665018-180115546.png
blocks.alt: Identical twins sharing the same genetic blueprint but existing as two separate individuals

blocks.content: A sharper version of this analogy: identical twins. Twins share the same DNA blueprint, practically the same "class." Yet they are unmistakably two different people, standing in two different places, capable of having two completely different days. If one twin gets a haircut, the other twin’s hair does not change. That is exactly how objects behave: shared structure (the class), independent state and identity (the object).
3. Problem It Solves & Definition

In software engineering terms, objects solve the problem of representing many independent, coexisting instances of the same concept at runtime. A banking app does not have one shared Account, it has millions of separate Account objects, each tracking its own balance. Objects also give you identity, a way to distinguish "this particular instance" from every other instance, even ones built from identical starting data.

blocks.title: Definition
blocks.content: An object is a runtime instantiation of a class, occupying its own region of memory, possessing a unique identity, and carrying its own independent copy of the fields defined by that class. In simple terms: an object is one instance of a class, created using the new keyword, with its own state stored in memory.
Notice the word identity in that definition. It is the single biggest thing that separates "an object" from "just some data", and it is the focus of most of this topic.
4. Key Terminology

["Object: a runtime instance of a class, also called an instance.","Identity: what makes one object distinguishable from another, even if their field values are identical, in Java this is tied to the object’s memory address.","Reference: a variable that points to an object’s location in memory, it does not contain the object itself.","Aliasing: when two or more reference variables point to the exact same object, changing the object through one reference is visible through the other.","Equality (equals): whether two objects are considered logically the \"same\" based on their data, independent of identity.","Identity comparison (equalequal in Java): whether two references point to the exact same object in memory.","Instantiation: the act of creating a new object using the new keyword.","Garbage collection: the JVM automatically freeing memory used by objects that are no longer reachable by any reference."]
items: Object: a runtime instance of a class, also called an instance.
Identity: what makes one object distinguishable from another, even if their field values are identical, in Java this is tied to the object’s memory address.
Reference: a variable that points to an object’s location in memory, it does not contain the object itself.
Aliasing: when two or more reference variables point to the exact same object, changing the object through one reference is visible through the other.
Equality (equals): whether two objects are considered logically the "same" based on their data, independent of identity.
Identity comparison (equalequal in Java): whether two references point to the exact same object in memory.
Instantiation: the act of creating a new object using the new keyword.
Garbage collection: the JVM automatically freeing memory used by objects that are no longer reachable by any reference.

blocks.alt: One Car class producing three separate objects, two with identical data and one with different data

6. Syntax & Code Example
Creating an object always follows the same shape, and accessing its fields or methods uses dot notation:

["new ClassName(...) is the only thing that actually creates a new object, everything else just refers to an already-existing one.","referenceVariable does not hold the object, it holds a pointer to where the object lives.","dot notation tells the runtime to follow the reference to the actual object and run that method on it."]
items: new ClassName(...) is the only thing that actually creates a new object, everything else just refers to an already-existing one.
referenceVariable does not hold the object, it holds a pointer to where the object lives.
dot notation tells the runtime to follow the reference to the actual object and run that method on it.

7. Code Breakdown

["Car car1 = new Car(...) and Car car2 = new Car(...) each call new, so each creates a genuinely separate object in memory, even though the constructor arguments are identical.","Car car3 = car1; this line creates NO new object at all, it simply copies the reference, so car3 now points to the exact same memory location as car1.","car1 == car2 compares identity (memory addresses), and since they are two different objects, this is false.","car1 == car3 compares identity too, and since car3 is just an alias for car1, this is true.","car1.equals(car2) uses the overridden equals method, which compares the vinNumber field instead of memory addresses, so it correctly returns true."]
items: Car car1 = new Car(...) and Car car2 = new Car(...) each call new, so each creates a genuinely separate object in memory, even though the constructor arguments are identical.
Car car3 = car1; this line creates NO new object at all, it simply copies the reference, so car3 now points to the exact same memory location as car1.
car1 == car2 compares identity (memory addresses), and since they are two different objects, this is false.
car1 == car3 compares identity too, and since car3 is just an alias for car1, this is true.
car1.equals(car2) uses the overridden equals method, which compares the vinNumber field instead of memory addresses, so it correctly returns true.

blocks.content: Here is exactly what happens at each step, and why:

Now let’s see exactly where these references and objects actually sit in memory:
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1784847670999-780889246.png
blocks.alt: car1 and car3 aliasing the same heap object while car2 is a separate object

blocks.content: 8.1 Reference Aliasing on the Stack

car1, car2, and car3 all live as reference variables on the stack. But car1 and car3 hold the exact same address value, they are aliases pointing at one shared object, while car2 holds a different address pointing at a second, independent object.
8.2 Two Real Objects on the Heap
blocks.text: 8.2 Two Real Objects on the Heap

blocks.content: Only two actual Car objects exist on the heap here, not three, because the new keyword was only called twice. The third variable, car3, is just another name for an object that already exists.
9. Behind the Scenes (JVM Internals)
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1784847672825-859020080.png
blocks.alt: Object header carrying identity information, and garbage collection sweeping unreachable objects

blocks.content: Every object the JVM creates carries a small internal object header alongside its field data, holding bookkeeping information (including what backs its identity hash) and a pointer to its class in the method area.
9.1 Identity Under the Hood

When Java computes a default hash code for an object (before any custom hashCode override), it is derived from this internal identity information, which is exactly why two objects with identical field values but different identities can still produce different default hash codes.
9.2 Garbage Collection

If every reference to an object disappears, for example a local variable goes out of scope and nothing else points to that object, the JVM’s garbage collector eventually detects the object is unreachable and frees its memory automatically. You never manually delete objects in Java, unlike in C++ where delete is explicit.
10. Real-World Use Cases & Industry Examples
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1784847674626-304217377.png
blocks.alt: Independent objects representing separate real entities across e-commerce, banking, social and gaming domains

blocks.content: ["E-commerce: every item added to a cart is its own object, so updating one item’s quantity never affects another item in the same cart.","Banking: every customer’s open session is backed by its own Account object, keeping balances isolated per user.","Social Media: every logged-in user has a distinct session object tracking their own feed state.","Gaming: every enemy on screen is a separate object with its own health and position, defeating one never affects the others."]
items: E-commerce: every item added to a cart is its own object, so updating one item’s quantity never affects another item in the same cart.
Banking: every customer’s open session is backed by its own Account object, keeping balances isolated per user.
Social Media: every logged-in user has a distinct session object tracking their own feed state.
Gaming: every enemy on screen is a separate object with its own health and position, defeating one never affects the others.

blocks.content: https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1784847676235-986347725.png
blocks.alt: Hibernate ORM mapping a single database row into one Car object in memory

blocks.content: Hibernate (and ORMs generally) work by turning each row fetched from a database table into exactly one object in memory, an @Entity-annotated Car class becomes one Car object per row. The Java Collections framework is built entirely around storing and retrieving objects: an ArrayList of Car simply holds a list of references to Car objects, not the objects inline.
11. Advantages & Limitations

{"headers":["Advantages","Limitations"],"rows":[["Independent state: each object manages its own data without interfering with others built from the same class.","Aliasing bugs: accidentally sharing a reference when you meant to create an independent copy can cause unexpected cross-effects."],["Identity tracking: you can tell two logically-similar things apart if they are genuinely different real-world entities.","Memory cost: every object carries some overhead, creating excessive short-lived objects can pressure the garbage collector."],["Automatic memory management: in Java, objects are reclaimed automatically once unreachable.","Equality confusion: without a properly overridden equals/hashCode, objects that \"look the same\" will not be treated as equal."]]}
12. Common Mistakes & Best Practices
12.1 Common Mistakes

["Using equalequal to check if two objects have \"the same data\" when equals() (or a custom comparison) is what is actually needed.","Assuming car3 = car1 makes a copy of the object, it only copies the reference, both variables point to one shared object.","Overriding equals() but forgetting to override hashCode() to match, which silently breaks hash-based collections like HashMap and HashSet.","Calling a method on a reference that is still null, causing a NullPointerException, always confirm an object was actually constructed before using it."]
items: Using equalequal to check if two objects have "the same data" when equals() (or a custom comparison) is what is actually needed.
Assuming car3 = car1 makes a copy of the object, it only copies the reference, both variables point to one shared object.
Overriding equals() but forgetting to override hashCode() to match, which silently breaks hash-based collections like HashMap and HashSet.
Calling a method on a reference that is still null, causing a NullPointerException, always confirm an object was actually constructed before using it.

blocks.content: 12.2 Best Practices

["Override both equals() and hashCode() together whenever an object needs to be compared by its data rather than its identity.","Be deliberate about aliasing, if a method should not be able to modify the caller’s object, pass a copy instead of the same reference.","Avoid creating throwaway objects inside tight loops when a reusable object would do, to reduce pressure on the garbage collector.","Give objects a clear, single identity concept (like a VIN or an ID field) whenever real-world uniqueness matters to the domain."]
items: Override both equals() and hashCode() together whenever an object needs to be compared by its data rather than its identity.
Be deliberate about aliasing, if a method should not be able to modify the caller’s object, pass a copy instead of the same reference.
Avoid creating throwaway objects inside tight loops when a reusable object would do, to reduce pressure on the garbage collector.
Give objects a clear, single identity concept (like a VIN or an ID field) whenever real-world uniqueness matters to the domain.

blocks.content: 13. Key Takeaways & Cheat Sheet

["An object is a runtime instance of a class, with its own state and a unique identity, even if its data happens to match another object’s.","A reference variable does not hold the object itself, it holds a pointer to it, copying a reference creates an alias, not a new object.","equalequal compares identity (same memory location), equals() compares logical data equality, these are frequently confused.","Only the new keyword creates a new object, everything else is just handing around references to objects that already exist.","The JVM automatically garbage collects objects once nothing references them anymore."]
items: An object is a runtime instance of a class, with its own state and a unique identity, even if its data happens to match another object’s.
A reference variable does not hold the object itself, it holds a pointer to it, copying a reference creates an alias, not a new object.
equalequal compares identity (same memory location), equals() compares logical data equality, these are frequently confused.
Only the new keyword creates a new object, everything else is just handing around references to objects that already exist.
The JVM automatically garbage collects objects once nothing references them anymore.

blocks.title: Interview tip
blocks.content: If asked "what is the difference between == and equals()", the fastest correct answer is: == checks whether two references point to the exact same object in memory, equals() checks whether two objects are logically equivalent based on their data, and the two frequently disagree unless equals() has been overridden.
